summary: Thalia or Thaleia (Ancient Greek Θάλεια, "the joyous, the abundance") was one of the fifty Nereids, marine-nymph daughters of Nereus and Doris. Homer names her among the Nereids who rise from the sea to mourn with Thetis for Achilles' grief over Patroclus; Virgil places her in Cyrene's train and among the Nereids who aid Aeneas in a storm.
etymology: Tháleia derives from thállein, "to flourish, to be green," hence "the joyous" or "the abundance" — a flourishing sea-nymph name shared with other divine Thalias.

sections.heading: In Homer and Virgil
paragraphs: In Iliad 18 Thaleia is listed among the thirty-three Nereids who gather on the Trojan shore when Thetis hears Achilles' cry for the dead Patroclus. She has no separate Homeric episode beyond that catalogue presence.
Virgil's Georgics sets Thalia with Cymodoce, Nesaea, and Spio in the train of Cyrene. In Aeneid 5 those four, with Thetis, Melite, and Panopea, help Aeneas and his crew through a storm.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: This node (thalia-nereid) is the Nereid only. She is not Thalia the Muse (thalia-muse), nor Thalia the Charis / Grace (thalia-charis). Same Greek name, different cosmic roles and atlas ids.
